“The American people deserve to know: did the secretary of commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise US national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” said Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California.

Cantor Fitzgerald insists it had “no role” in the Trump administration’s decisions about Nvidia.

But in a letter on Tuesday to Lutnick’s son Brandon, who now serves as chair of Cantor Fitzgerald, the trio of lawmakers demanded documents and records, including communications concerning Nvidia.

They said that they wanted to “understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.

Raskin is the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives. Meeks is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs committee. Kamlager-Dove is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs subcommittee on south and central Asia.

In an accompanying news release, the lawmakers said that they were seeking to determine whether Lutnick “blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock”.

Howard Lutnick led Cantor Fitzgerald until his confirmation as commerce secretary in February 2025, when he transferred his stake in the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children.

In the letter to Brandon Lutnick, the lawmakers wrote that at the time of Howard Lutnick’s confirmation, Cantor Fitzgerald had “amassed a significant stake” in Nvidia, reportedly “holding more than 3.5m shares, valued at over $1.3bn”.

In a statement to the Guardian, a Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson said that the claims in the letter were “inaccurate”. “Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia,” the spokesperson said. “Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients.

“The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position,” the statement continued. “Allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless. Additionally, Cantor has no role in US export control or entity list decisions [to determine trade restrictions].”

The Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson also said that they were “confident that a full review of the facts will demonstrate that we have operated our business ethically and in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations”.

A commerce department spokesperson told the Times that Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the US and that he does not discuss department matters with his sons. The spokesperson added that Lutnick’s sons also do not discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him.

item.title: I, too, was raped by my partner while drugged and unconscious. There are more survivors than you think | Zoe Watts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: personal narrative, clear and impactful

Like many, I followed closely the sickening case of Philip Young, who has been convicted of repeatedly drugging and raping his now ex-wife, Joanne Young, and advertising her on the internet for sex. It is, to any right-thinking person, unimaginably horrific that the person you’re supposed to trust most in the world would betray you in this, the worst possible way.

I don’t have to imagine it, however. I have lived it. The man I had been with since I was 17 – my husband and the father of my four children, the man who had vowed to love and look after me and with whom I had shared a bed for almost 7,000 nights – did the same to me.

Since Gisèle Pelicot stepped out of the shadows and waived her right to anonymity, the depraved crime of drug-facilitated sexual abuse has become stamped into the public’s consciousness – rightly provoking outrage and an outpouring of support for survivors.

My experience, some two years before Pelicot’s trial, was different. There was just one single perpetrator, my husband.

I have no idea how many times it happened, nor do I wish to know, but for years he had been crushing sleeping pills into the cup of tea he made for me every night, then waiting for me to lose consciousness before raping me, often taking photographs and filming himself in the act.

There was no outpouring of support when I finally reported the crime. Quite the opposite, in fact. I was ostracised and publicly accused of destroying the reputation of this upstanding pillar of the community. This continued, inexplicably, even after his conviction.

The police were brilliant. The CPS less so. I had to fight to press charges when, after 18 months, it announced it was not going to, even though he had admitted his guilt to medical professionals. I felt as though I was the one on trial rather than him, and the verdict was already in. How could it be true? How could I not have known?

In truth I didn’t, but in hindsight the warning signs had been there: recurrent and unexplained bouts of thrush and urinary tract infections, worsening migraines, and just the nagging feeling that something in my body wasn’t quite right.

The reality was so unimaginable that even when he sat me down and told me what he had been doing, one day after church, it was as though my brain couldn’t process what he was saying. It was months before I told my sister and mum, who gently persuaded me to talk to the police, and it was only then I started to see that what he had been doing – each act – was a crime. A violation of my body, trust and everything I had believed to be true.

It is only recently that I’ve been able to bring myself to call it what it was – rape – and understand (something many survivors struggle with) that just because I can’t remember it, doesn’t mean it didn’t happen. Just because it was my husband doesn’t mean it didn’t count.

I don’t think this type of crime is becoming more common, I think the reporting of it is. The drugs used might be more sophisticated, so, too, the means by which perpetrators communicate with each other and share images and video. The crime, however, has always been there behind closed doors.

Prior to the Pelicot case, this kind of crime was virtually unheard of. What Pelicot did was open the door for people to think that a man could do that to his wife. She created a space in which people could ask questions and could stand up and say, “This has happened to me as well.”

What none of us could have anticipated is the scale. Through #EndEyeCheck, the campaign publicly launched in May this year by fellow survivor-advocate Amanda Stanhope and me, we now know that this has happened and is still happening to hundreds of women around the world – and that doesn’t include those who haven’t yet had that realisation or don’t deem it rape.

The campaign name comes from a term I was blissfully unaware of before all this happened – used to describe the moment an abuser pulls back or lifts the eyelid of their victim to check they are fully unconscious before sexually assaulting them.

Stories such as ours shine a light on this crime, but that is not enough and nor are the sentences handed down. My ex was given 11 years, and I’ll be lucky if he serves the same length of time in prison that his offences span. The government must act now to protect victims.

There needs to be earlier, more effective education around consent, starting in schools, so there can be no confusion and no blurring of boundaries over what is and isn’t allowed. I remember hearing teenage boys on the bus discussing CNC (consensual non-consent) porn and thinking, “Do they even know what it stands for or what it means?”

The platforms, mainstream porn sites among them, that are hosting this almost innocent-sounding “sleep content” must be held to account. It is not innocent – it is perpetuating the idea that consent is not obligatory.

The medical profession and the police also need to be alive to the signs of this type of abuse because the chances are the victims haven’t yet realised what is happening to them and may not, without informed support.

Like many, Pelicot inspired me and played a huge part in the decision to waive my anonymity. It’s not for everyone, but in a strange kind of way it helped me to heal and imagine a future that, at one point, seemed impossible.

It is a complex problem and there is no easy answer, but at least now the conversation has started – and there is a place for women to go for help and to know they are not alone.

- Zoe Watts is a campaigner and cofounder of the #EndEyeCheck campaign to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse…

item.title: China’s Downstream Nations Need a Collective Voice
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

China is building the world’s largest hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet, designed with a massive 60,000-megawatt capacity. Construction was formally launched in July 2025, much to the consternation of people across the border in India.

“China has already begun construction of a dam in Medog County, around 40 km from the border… without consulting us or sharing any information,” warned Chief Minister Pema Khandu of Arunachal Pradesh. He called China’s $167 billion mega-dam in a seismically active zone an existential potential “water bomb.”

The Medog dam is not an isolated incident. It’s just one sign of a larger crisis extending across Asia’s river basins, where downstream nations face upper-riparian infrastructure that proceeds unilaterally, without environmental impact disclosures, binding legal frameworks, or genuine transboundary consultation and governance.

Downstream states urgently need a collective voice, built on shared demands for data and transparency.

Known as the “Water Tower of Asia,” Tibet is the source of 10 major transboundary river systems that flow into 10 downstream nations. These vital waterways sustain ecosystems, agriculture, and the livelihoods of 1.8 billion people across South and Southeast Asia, nearly one-quarter of the global population. No other single territory matches this human impact in supplying transboundary freshwater to densely populated downstream nations. That gives Tibet an unparalleled position in global hydrology.

Tibet also stores more freshwater than any place on earth apart from the two poles, which is why it is often referred to as the Third Pole of the planet. However, Tibet faces a dual crisis: it is warming at roughly twice the global average while its high-altitude environment is also continually battered by mining, deforestation, and industrial activity – a combination that threatens the stability of Asia’s major rivers.

Tibet’s glaciers, permafrost, wetlands, lakes, and high-altitude ecosystems regulate water availability and influence downstream hydrological and ecological processes. Large-scale damming on these rivers, much of it is in highly seismic terrain and without transparency or treaty frameworks, deepens downstream uncertainty over water flows and flooding risks that cross borders.

China rejects these concerns outright. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun stated that China has carried out cooperation with downstream countries and has had necessary communication with them. The spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in India, Yu Jing, insisted that the dam project on the Yarlung Tsangpo will not have a negative impact on the ecological environment, geological conditions, and the rights and interests related to water resources of downstream countries. Rather, she claimed that it will “to some extent, help with their disaster prevention and reduction and climate response.”

However, downstream nations have deep concern about the absence of binding agreements. China voted against the 1997 U.N. Watercourses Convention and has no binding water-sharing treaty with its neighbors, while the non-binding memoranda that once underpinned data-sharing have lapsed. Many analysts therefore fear that China could weaponize Tibet’s water and assume the role of “Asia’s water hegemon,” driven largely by its favorable geopolitical position.

As China controls the headwaters of three major Indian river systems – the Brahmaputra, Indus, and Sutlej – opaque upstream water governance has become an acute national security concern for India. China has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to weaponize water transparency. During the Doklam standoff in 2017, China abruptly halted providing crucial monsoon-season water-flow data for the Yarlung Tsangpo (which becomes the Brahmaputra in India), citing station upgrades, an explanation many Indian analysts doubted as it was sharing the same data with Bangladesh. Cooperation has since eroded further, with the expiration of bilateral data-sharing agreements on the Sutlej in 2020 and the Brahmaputra in 2023.

Now, China is building the world’s largest mega-dam on a seismically volatile fault roughly 40 kilometers from the Indian border, risking catastrophic flooding across Arunachal Pradesh and Assam and endangering millions of lives. The 2000 Yigong dam breach in Tibet showed how violently upstream surges can hit downstream countries – the ensuing flood displaced 50,000 people across Arunachal Pradesh and Assam.

In 2024, 10-Point Call from Tibetan Experts in India demanded full environmental transparency for the downstream nations, immediate halt to large hydropower projects lacking local consent, and adhere to Free, Prior, and Informed Consent to prevent forced relocations and cultural destruction in Tibet.

India is not alone in expressing concerns about China’s unilateral approach to water issues. It’s also a recurring point of frustration for Southeast Asian countries on the Mekong River, known as the Lancang in China.

In 2016, a severe drought hit the Mekong Delta in Vietnam. The Stimson Center later published satellite-based evidence that upstream dam operations in China restricted river flow even when the upper basin recorded above-average rain and snowmelt. During this upstream squeeze, 166,000 hectares of rice-growing land was rendered infertile, leaving 2 million people without adequate drinking water. The Vietnam’s Ministry of Agriculture estimated that $4 billion was required to combat the drought and salinization in the Delta region.

Mekong River Commission (MRC) projections warn that cumulative damming could cut total delta sediment by up to 97 percent by 2040. Moreover, according to the World Wildlife Fund, the Mekong Giant Catfish stocks declined by 90 percent over the past two decades – a warning that could slash the world’s fourth largest fishing industry.…
